tribology-001.question: Which statement correctly describes the empirical law of friction (the Amontons–Coulomb law) that often holds for dry sliding friction between metals?
choices: Friction force is proportional to the apparent contact area, so doubling the contact area at the same load roughly doubles the friction force
Friction force is roughly proportional to the normal load and hardly depends on the apparent contact area
Friction force increases in proportion to the sliding speed, and static friction is smaller than kinetic friction
tribology-001.explanation: Under the Amontons–Coulomb law, the friction force F is proportional to the normal load W (F = μW) and depends little on the apparent contact area or the sliding speed. A surface carries tiny asperities, and only their tips actually touch. Because the asperities deform plastically to support the load, the real area of contact equals the load divided by the hardness and is proportional to the load regardless of the apparent area. The friction force is proportional to this real area of contact, so it ends up proportional to the load. The idea that friction scales with the apparent area confuses the real area of contact with the apparent area. Proportionality to speed is a property of viscous resistance in fluids, and in dry friction the static friction coefficient is generally larger than the kinetic one.

tribology-002.question: A flat steel block (indentation hardness H = 2.0 GPa) rests on a plate of the same steel, and a normal load of 1.0 kN is applied over an apparent contact area of 10 cm². Assuming every contacting asperity deforms plastically and estimating the real area of contact as Ar = W/H, which is closest to its fraction of the apparent contact area?
choices: About 0.5%
About 50%
About 0.05%
tribology-002.explanation: Ar = W/H = 1.0×10³/(2.0×10⁹) = 5.0×10⁻⁷ m² = 0.50 mm². The apparent area is 10 cm² = 1000 mm², so the fraction is 0.50/1000 = 5×10⁻⁴, about 0.05%. Even on a surface that looks flat, only a tiny part at the asperity tips actually touches, and those spots carry a high pressure equal to the hardness. About 0.5% is the value obtained by converting 1 cm² as 10 mm² instead of 100 mm², and about 50% is the value obtained by treating the hardness in MPa instead of GPa. The high local pressure at the real contact spots, together with the high temperature generated by sliding, is the starting point for adhesion and wear.

tribology-003.question: In the adhesion theory (the view of Bowden and Tabor), the friction force is set by the force needed to shear the adhesive junctions at the real contact spots, and the friction coefficient is μ = s/H (s is the shear strength of the junctions and H is the indentation hardness of the softer material). For s = 0.30 GPa and H = 1.8 GPa, which is closest to μ?
choices: About 0.17
About 6.0
About 0.50
tribology-003.explanation: μ = s/H = 0.30/1.8 ≈ 0.17. The friction force is the product F = sAr of the real area of contact Ar = W/H and the junction shear strength s, so F/W = s/H, giving a friction coefficient that depends neither on the load nor on the apparent area. About 6.0 is the value with numerator and denominator swapped, and about 0.50 is the value obtained by dividing by the yield stress estimate H/3 = 0.60 GPa instead of the hardness. Between real metals, the growth of junctions under combined load and shear (junction growth) and ploughing by hard asperities add to this, so μ is often larger than 0.17. The formula also shows that lowering the shear strength s with a lubricant film or an oxide film lowers μ.

tribology-004.question: Which of the following descriptions of wear mechanisms corresponds to adhesive wear?
choices: Hard particles or hard asperities on the counterface scratch and cut material away from a softer surface
Contact stresses repeated in rolling contact and the like create cracks below the surface, and the surface layer comes off in small flakes
Metals bond strongly at the real contact spots, and when sliding shears the junctions, material from one side transfers to the other or detaches to form wear debris
tribology-004.explanation: Adhesive wear occurs when surface atoms bond at the real contact spots (microscopic welding), and when sliding shears the junctions, material tears out of the weaker side, transfers to the counterface and eventually detaches as wear debris. It is severe between clean metals of the same kind and in bad cases leads to seizure. It can be reduced by pairing metals with little mutual solubility, and by lubricants and oxide films. Hard particles or asperities cutting a surface is abrasive wear, and cracks growing from below the surface under repeated contact stress until flakes come off is fatigue wear (fatigue pits and spalling), seen in bearings and gears. In real wear, several of these mechanisms often act at the same time.

tribology-005.question: A construction-machine part is rubbed by soil containing quartz sand grains (hardness about 1000 HV). Which is the correct way to choose a material that reduces abrasive wear?
choices: Raising the surface hardness to about that of the sand grains or higher makes it hard for the grains to dig into the surface and reduces wear greatly
Martensite in hardened steel is harder than quartz, so simply hardening the steel makes wear almost disappear
The amount of abrasive wear is set by the sliding distance alone and does not depend on the surface hardness
tribology-005.explanation: Empirically, a grain must be about 1.2 times harder than the surface (Ha ≥ about 1.2Hs) to scratch it, and once the surface hardness Hs is raised so that Hs/Ha exceeds about 0.8, abrasive wear drops sharply. The grains can no longer dig into the surface, and their corners are crushed instead. For this reason, high-chromium cast irons containing much Cr carbide (about 1200–1800 HV), which is harder than quartz, hardfacing welds containing WC, and ceramic coatings are used. Martensite in hardened steel is around 900 HV even at high carbon, about as hard as quartz or softer, so it raises wear resistance but does not eliminate wear. The amount of wear is proportional to the sliding distance, but hardness also has a large effect, so it is not independent of hardness.

tribology-006.question: In a pin-on-disk test, a pin of hardness H = 2.0 GPa is loaded with a normal force of 50 N and slid over a distance of 1.0 km. Using the Archard wear equation V = KWL/H with a dimensionless wear coefficient K = 1.0×10⁻⁴, which correctly pairs the wear volume of the pin with the change in wear volume when the load is doubled?
choices: About 2.5×10⁻³ mm³, and doubling the load roughly doubles it
About 2.5 mm³, and doubling the load roughly doubles it
About 2.5 mm³, and doubling the load leaves it unchanged as long as the apparent contact area is the same
tribology-006.explanation: V = KWL/H = 1.0×10⁻⁴×50×1000/(2.0×10⁹) = 2.5×10⁻⁹ m³ = 2.5 mm³. The Archard equation assumes that a number of contact spots proportional to the real area of contact W/H produce wear debris a number of times proportional to the sliding distance, so the wear volume is proportional to the load and the sliding distance and inversely proportional to the hardness. Doubling the load doubles the real area of contact even if the apparent contact area stays the same, so the wear volume also roughly doubles. About 2.5×10⁻³ mm³ is the value calculated with the sliding distance taken as 1 instead of 1000 m. K varies widely, from about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻², with the wear mechanism and conditions, so it is determined by experiment.

tribology-007.question: Which statement correctly describes the Stribeck curve, which plots the friction coefficient of a plain bearing against the bearing characteristic number ηN/P formed from the lubricant viscosity η, the rotational speed N and the bearing pressure P?
choices: In the boundary-to-mixed lubrication region where ηN/P is small, increasing ηN/P lowers the friction coefficient, and in the hydrodynamic lubrication region past the minimum, it rises gently because of the viscous resistance of the oil
The friction coefficient is largest in the hydrodynamic lubrication region and smallest in the boundary lubrication region, where the oil film breaks and solids touch
The friction coefficient is nearly constant regardless of ηN/P, and the lubrication regime is set by the bearing pressure alone
tribology-007.explanation: When ηN/P is small, that is, at low speed, high pressure and low viscosity, the oil film is thin and asperities touch, giving boundary lubrication with a large friction coefficient of about 0.1. As ηN/P increases, the bearing passes through mixed lubrication, in which pressure in the oil film generated by the wedge effect carries part of the load, and reaches hydrodynamic lubrication, in which the oil film fully separates the surfaces, and the friction coefficient falls to about 0.001–0.01. Raising the speed further in the hydrodynamic region increases the viscous resistance from shearing the oil, so the friction coefficient rises gently. The statement that friction is smallest in boundary lubrication has it backward, and the lubrication regime depends not only on pressure but also on viscosity and speed. A bearing runs stably when operated slightly on the hydrodynamic side of the minimum.

tribology-008.question: In a rolling bearing, the minimum oil film thickness is h = 0.40 µm and the root-mean-square roughnesses of the two surfaces are Rq1 = 0.15 µm and Rq2 = 0.20 µm. Find the film thickness ratio λ = h/√(Rq1² + Rq2²) and, taking λ < 1 as boundary lubrication, 1–3 as mixed lubrication and above 3 as hydrodynamic (full-film) lubrication, choose the correct pairing.
choices: λ ≈ 6.4, full-film lubrication
λ ≈ 0.63, boundary lubrication
λ ≈ 1.6, mixed lubrication
tribology-008.explanation: The composite roughness is √(0.15² + 0.20²) = √0.0625 = 0.25 µm, so λ = 0.40/0.25 = 1.6, which by the guideline is mixed lubrication. When the film thickness is about 1–3 times the composite roughness, asperities touch here and there, and the load is shared between film pressure and asperity contact. λ ≈ 6.4 is the value obtained by dividing by 0.0625 without taking the square root, and λ ≈ 0.63 is the value with numerator and denominator swapped, dividing the composite roughness by the film thickness. λ can be raised by using a more viscous oil or by finishing the surfaces more smoothly to reduce roughness, which is effective in extending rolling bearing life. The boundary values are empirical guidelines and differ somewhat between sources.

tribology-009.question: A plain bearing with an inner diameter of 40 mm and a width of 30 mm carries a radial load of 1.2 kN, and the shaft turns at 600 rpm. Taking the bearing pressure P as the load divided by the projected area (inner diameter × width) and the sliding speed v as the surface speed of the shaft, which is closest to the PV value?
choices: About 75 MPa·m/s
About 1.3 MPa·m/s
About 0.40 MPa·m/s
tribology-009.explanation: The bearing pressure is P = 1.2×10³/(0.040×0.030) = 1.0×10⁶ Pa = 1.0 MPa and the surface speed is v = π×0.040×600/60 ≈ 1.26 m/s, so PV ≈ 1.0×1.26 ≈ 1.3 MPa·m/s. Frictional heat generated per unit area is μPV, so the PV value is a guide to temperature rise and wear in a bearing, and allowable values are set for each material in polymer bearings and sintered oil-impregnated bearings. About 75 MPa·m/s is the value obtained by using 600 as is without converting the rotational speed to revolutions per second. About 0.40 MPa·m/s is the value obtained by dividing the load by the circumferential area πDL instead of the projected area. Even when the PV value is within its limit, also check that P and v each stay below their own limits.

tribology-010.question: Why is molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) better suited than graphite as a solid lubricant for mechanisms used in vacuum, such as on satellites?
choices: MoS₂ is harder than graphite, so it survives longer in vacuum without being worn away

The easy sliding between graphite layers is assisted by adsorbed water molecules and the like, so friction rises in vacuum, whereas MoS₂ has inherently weak bonding between layers and keeps low friction in vacuum
Graphite sublimes in vacuum and quickly disappears
tribology-010.explanation: Graphite and MoS₂ are both layered crystals that give low friction because layers stacked by weak van der Waals forces slide over one another. In graphite, however, water molecules and gases adsorbed at layer edges and elsewhere help the layers slide, so in vacuum or dry gas the friction coefficient becomes large and wear increases. MoS₂ layers slide easily by nature, with a low friction coefficient of about 0.05 or less in vacuum, so it is used in space hardware. Conversely, in humid air MoS₂ oxidizes easily and its performance drops. Both are soft materials and are not chosen for hardness. Graphite is lost by sublimation only at high temperatures above about 2000 °C, which is not a concern at the temperatures where mechanisms operate.

tribology-011.question: A gear made of low-carbon steel (about 0.2%C) is carburized and quenched. Which statement about this treatment is correct?
choices: Carbon is diffused into the surface layer in the austenite region (about 900–950 °C), which can dissolve much carbon, and the part is then quenched so the surface becomes hard high-carbon martensite while the core keeps a tough low-carbon structure
Carburizing is done in the ferrite region (about 550 °C), which can dissolve much carbon, so the surface hardens without quenching and distortion is small
Raising the carbon content of the surface layer leaves tensile residual stress in the surface after quenching, so the fatigue strength of the gear drops
tribology-011.explanation: Carburizing is done in the austenite region (about 900–950 °C), where carbon solubility is large (about 1.2–1.4% in the 900 °C range) and diffusion is fast. When the surface carbon content is raised to around 0.8% and the part is quenched, the surface becomes hard martensite and the core a tough low-carbon structure, combining wear resistance with impact resistance. The carbon-rich surface has a lower martensite start temperature and transforms later than the core, so its volume expansion is constrained by the core and compressive residual stress remains in the surface, which also raises fatigue strength. The solubility limit of carbon in ferrite is at most about 0.02%, and hardening without quenching in the low-temperature ferrite region is a feature of nitriding. Carburizing and quenching requires measures against quench distortion.

tribology-012.question: Which statement about nitriding, such as gas nitriding, applied to a nitriding steel containing Al, Cr and Mo is correct?
choices: Nitrogen is diffused in the austenite region and the part is then quenched to martensite, so it shows larger quench distortion than carburizing and quenching
Pure iron and carbon steels without alloying elements that combine readily with nitrogen form the hardest nitrided layers

Nitrogen is diffused in the ferrite region at about 500–570 °C, below the A₁ transformation temperature, and the surface is hardened by precipitation of fine alloy nitrides, so no quenching is needed and dimensional change and distortion are small
tribology-012.explanation: Nitriding introduces nitrogen from the surface, for example by decomposing ammonia, and is carried out at about 500–570 °C, below the A₁ transformation temperature (727 °C). Nitrogen diffuses through ferrite and combines with Al, Cr, Mo, V and similar elements to form fine nitrides, and the surface reaches hardnesses above 1000 HV. With no phase transformation or quenching, dimensional change and distortion are small, so parts can be treated after finish machining. A compound layer of iron nitrides (the white layer) forms at the outermost surface, with a diffusion layer beneath it. Carbon steels without alloying elements form few hard fine nitrides, so their hardness does not rise much. On the other hand, the case is about 0.1–0.5 mm, thinner than with carburizing, and treatment often takes several tens of hours, which are drawbacks.

tribology-013.question: Which statement correctly describes electroless nickel plating (Ni-P plating)?
choices: It becomes thick at corners and edges where current concentrates and hardly deposits deep inside holes, so it is unsuited to parts of complex shape
Because it contains phosphorus it never becomes amorphous, and heat treatment at about 400 °C drives out the phosphorus and softens it

It deposits autocatalytically through a reducing agent (hypophosphite) in the bath without an external power supply, so it forms a nearly uniform thickness even on parts of complex shape, and heat treatment increases its hardness
tribology-013.explanation: In electroless nickel plating, hypophosphite in the bath reduces nickel ions, and the deposited nickel itself catalyzes the reaction so that growth continues. Because it is not governed by current distribution, it deposits with uniform thickness inside holes and on parts of complex shape, and with suitable pretreatment it can even plate nonconductors such as plastics. The deposit contains a few to over ten percent phosphorus, and high-phosphorus deposits are amorphous. Heat treatment at about 400 °C precipitates Ni₃P and raises the hardness from about 500 HV to about 900–1000 HV. Thickening at corners and edges and poor coverage deep in holes are properties of electroplating, which passes a current. Heat treatment does not drive out the phosphorus and soften the deposit.

tribology-014.question: Cutting tools are coated with hard films such as TiN. Which is an appropriate way to choose the coating method for cemented carbide tools and for high-speed tool steel (HSS) tools?
choices: HSS has higher heat resistance than cemented carbide, so coating it by thermal CVD at about 1000 °C does not lower its hardness

Cemented carbide can be given thick, well-adhering films by thermal CVD at about 1000 °C, but HSS is coated by PVD, which can run at about 500 °C or below, so as not to exceed its tempering temperature (about 550 °C)
PVD uses no chemical reaction, so it cannot make compound films such as TiN and can only deposit metal films
tribology-014.explanation: Thermal CVD forms films by reacting source gases such as TiCl₄, N₂ and H₂ at about 1000 °C. It gives thick, well-adhering films and is widely used for cemented carbide tools, which do not soften at high temperature. HSS gets its hardness from quenching and tempering, so heating above the tempering temperature softens it, and requenching also raises problems of dimensional change. PVD methods such as sputtering and arc ion plating are therefore used at about 500 °C or below. Even with PVD, compound films such as TiN, TiAlN and CrN can be made by reactive deposition, in which Ti is evaporated or sputtered in a nitrogen-containing atmosphere. The heat resistance of HSS is lower than that of cemented carbide, and it cannot withstand thermal CVD temperatures.

tribology-015.question: The hardness of a TiN film 2.0 µm thick is measured by indentation with a Vickers indenter. To avoid influence from the substrate, the empirical guideline of keeping the indentation depth to one tenth of the film thickness or less is used. The depth of a Vickers indent is about one seventh of its diagonal length. Which is closest to the largest allowable diagonal length?
choices: About 1.4 µm
About 0.20 µm
About 14 µm
tribology-015.explanation: The upper limit on indentation depth is 2.0/10 = 0.20 µm, and since the depth is about 1/7 of the diagonal, the upper limit on the diagonal is 0.20×7 = 1.4 µm. Indenting deeper also deforms the softer substrate beneath the film, giving a value lower than the hardness of the film alone. About 0.20 µm is the value obtained by mistaking the depth limit for the diagonal length, and about 14 µm is the value obtained by indenting all the way to the film thickness without using the one-tenth guideline. A 1.4 µm diagonal is hard to read accurately with an optical microscope, so the hardness of thin films is usually found by nanoindentation, which continuously measures load and indentation depth. The one-tenth value is a guideline and changes with the ratio of film to substrate hardness.
